newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Crisis sends Bulgarian lev into free fall.
newsitem.headline: Crisis sends Bulgarian lev into free fall.

text.p: Shopkeepers selling imported goods revised their prices every hour on Thursday as a crisis of confidence sent the Bulgarian currency into free fall against the dollar.
In one electronic goods shop displaying a sign warning: "prices in levs do not apply", manager Vladimir Angelov said he had stopped ordering new stock.
"I'm happy we are not selling much because I'm not sure at what rate I will have to buy currency tomorrow," he said.
Many exchange bureaus stopped selling dollars as they were unsure what rate to use. A rumour swept the foreign exchange market that the bureaux would be closed to limit dollar sales.
"To import anything in Bulgaria now is masochism," said Georgi Danev, selling stereo equipment.
"We are living in an absurd situation, I am updating my prices every hour and still I am not sure whether I will be in the black at the end of the day."

Businessmen at foreign companies said they were watching developments with great concern. The lev, which began the week at 272-275 on Monday, closed on Thursday down 60 at 395, a loss of 18 percent on the day.

"Suppliers are waiting to see how the situation stabilises, very little business is actually being done," said one foreign businessman. "People are waiting to see whether the lev stabilises or continues in free fall.
"We'll still continue to do business but pricing is a bit of a problem."
Since last week, depositors have withdrawn some 14.4 billion levs from the State Savings Bank, the country's largest savings institution.

Some 75 percent of its deposits are invested in Treasury paper and depositors feared the finance ministry might suspend payments on government securities under a currency board system being discussed for Bulgaria.
Asked whether the lev decline was due just to panic among depositors, Filipov said there were also fundamental problems with the heavily-indebted economy.

Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997 and debt markets speculate that Bulgaria could become the first country to default on a Brady debt restructuring deal.
BNB foreign exchange reserves reserves stood near $541 million at the end of October, down from $1.434 billion a year ago. The central bank also manages gold reserves worth some $400 million.
Bulgaria has the lowest rate of foreign investment in the region and has lagged behind other countries in implementing reforms since the end of communist rule in 1989.
"We're seeing the natural conclusion being played out of six years of nothing -- no reforms, no development, no investment," said the foreign businessman.

The International Monetary Fund has proposed a currency board to stabilise the economy by forcing Bulgaria to match levs in circulation with foreign exchange reserves, pegging the currency to the dollar or the mark.

Reaction to the proposal has been mixed. While many traders say they would welcome a more predictable exchange rate, the central bank fears a loss of sovereignty, and some businessmen fear it could dry up trade by causing an initial shortage of foreign currency.
Details of how a currency board would work have yet to be settled, and the question of who should run it and how much independence it will be allowed has attracted much speculation.
